## The defect

`PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:428`) flushes the checkpoint-ref push queue with no OPF (OpenAI Privacy Filter) gate. Its only production caller is the migration command's opt-in push (`cmd/entire/cli/doctor_migrate.go:100`), so with `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled` set, answering yes to the "Push N migrated checkpoint ref(s) now?" prompt sends 8-layer content to the remote, untagged.

The pre-push path a few lines above does gate it:

```go
// prePushCheckpointRefs, manual_commit_push.go:399
if redact.OPFEnabled() && !runOPFForCheckpointRefs(ctx, repo) {
    return nil
}
```

`PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` goes straight from the checkpoint-policy check to `flushCheckpointRefsQueue`, and that function has no OPF or redaction call of its own, so nothing downstream compensates.

## Why it matters, stated precisely

Un-OPF'd content reaching the remote is not itself the bug. `runOPFForCheckpointRefs` (`manual_commit_push.go:239`) has three outcomes: `OPFRun` rewrites, `OPFAbort` withholds, and `OPFSkip` deliberately flushes 8-layer content as-is and untagged when the user opts out for that push. The bug is that this path hard-codes the skip outcome without the decision ever being resolved or surfaced. A user who enabled OPF and never chose to skip gets the skip anyway.

The two answers to one prompt have opposite safety:
- No: "Refs stay queued for the next push", and the next `git push` goes through `prePushCheckpointRefs`, which applies OPF.
- Yes: they go now, without it.

## Scope

- git-refs checkpoint backend only. The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch has its own OPF rewrite at pre-push and is unaffected.
- Needs `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled` plus an interactive confirmation, so not unprompted. But the prompt says nothing about redaction, so there is nothing for the user to notice.
- Pre-existing. Not introduced by any currently open PR. Found while security-reviewing #2211, which is unrelated to it.

## Verified vs not

Verified by reading current `origin/main`: the gate exists at `:399` and is absent at `:428`; `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` contains no OPF/redact reference; `doctor_migrate.go:100` is the sole production caller; the four existing tests (`strategy/refs_push_test.go:208,230,258,285`) cover push-disabled, policy-blocked, and failure-leaves-refs-queued, none cover OPF.

NOT verified: no end-to-end run was done proving un-redacted bytes land on a remote. Worth doing before the PR claims it.

## Suggested fix, and a caveat about it

Give `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` the same gate as `prePushCheckpointRefs`, but keep the asymmetry in what failing closed means: the pre-push path must never block the user's `git push`, so it withholds the flush and returns nil; this path is an explicitly requested push and can return an error with the refs left queued, matching how it already handles a blocking checkpoint policy. Plus a test that enables OPF and asserts the flush is withheld when the rewrite fails.

Caveat worth taking seriously: in a recent issue (#2197) the triage session prescribed a fix that turned out to be unsafe, and a contributor implemented it faithfully before anyone caught it. Treat the paragraph above as a starting hypothesis to check against the code, not a spec. In particular confirm that returning an error here cannot break `doctor_migrate.go`'s own error handling at `:100-115`.

Constraints: do not post to GitHub, do not push. Do not use `git stash` (shared stack across worktrees). Work in your own worktree.
</cross-session-message>

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Done and verified. Here's what I found and changed.

## The defect is real, and I proved it end-to-end

Everything in the handoff checked out against `origin/main`. The one item marked NOT verified — that un-OPF'd bytes actually reach a remote — is now verified. A RED test against unmodified code showed `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs`, with OPF enabled, pushing both checkpoint refs to a bare remote with **zero** OPF invocations and no `Entire-OPF-Applied` trailer on the commits that landed. A second test showed a deliberately failing OPF runtime didn't stop the push either.

## The fix

`runOPFForCheckpointRefs` (bool) became `opfGateForCheckpointRefs` (error) at `manual_commit_push.go:249`. It resolves the decision and runs the rewrite; reporting moves to the caller, because the two callers need opposite failure surfaces:

- `prePushCheckpointRefs:407` — warns and returns nil, unchanged. A checkpoint failure must never block the user's own `git push`.
- `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs:455` — returns an error with the refs left queued, matching the checkpoint-policy branch three lines above it.

Both `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` call sites are now behind the gate; I confirmed there are only two, and that the v1 path's rewrite has only its one guarded call site.

## On the caveat you flagged

I checked `doctor_migrate.go:100-115` rather than assuming. The error is wrapped with `%w`, so its `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)` → `NewSilentError` branch still matches; otherwise it wraps as `push migrated refs: …`, exits non-zero, and the refs stay queued for the next `git push`, which applies OPF. Nothing breaks.

**One behaviour change worth putting in the PR description:** `doctor migrate` only reaches this code when a TTY is present, so answering yes to "Push N migrated checkpoint ref(s) now?" with OPF enabled now shows a second prompt — the standard "Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints?" — unless `prompt_default` or `ENTIRE_OPF` already decides it. That second prompt is the point: it's the decision that was previously hard-coded to skip.

## Verification

`mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean (0 issues), and full `mise run test:ci` passes — unit, integration, and the Vogon canary E2E (4/4). The four pre-existing `TestPushQueuedCheckpointRefs*` tests still pass alongside the two new ones.

I left the work uncommitted in this worktree (`worktree/calm-harbor-6f61`) since neither you nor the peer asked for a commit — say the word and I'll commit it. Two files changed: `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go` and `refs_push_test.go`. No pushes, no GitHub posts.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

- The fix adds the gate at each CALL SITE of `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` (there are two). content.text:
Four reviewers, deduped and applied. `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean, full `test:ci` green, and I re-confirmed both tests still fail with the gate removed — the rework didn't hollow them out.

## Fixed

**Production** — `manual_commit_push.go` is now *smaller* than before this cleanup:
- `redact.OPFEnabled()` moved inside `opfGateForCheckpointRefs` as an early return. Both call sites collapse from a nested double-`if` to one line, and a future third caller can no longer half-apply the gate by remembering the function but forgetting the flag. Simplification and altitude reviewers both pointed here.
- Cut the 6-line call-site comment in `PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` — every clause was already in the gate's doc, the function's doc, or the error string on the next line.
- Cut the sentence narrating the change's history rather than the code.

**Tests** — net smaller and materially stronger:
- Both tests moved onto the existing `setupGitRefsOPFRepo` fixture, which writes sentinel-bearing sessions through the real backend. The success test now asserts the sentinel is actually **scrubbed** and that the *rewritten* object is what reached the remote — not merely that a trailer is present. That's a better test than the one I wrote.
- Deleted my hand-rolled `remoteCommitMessage` (`testutil.RunGit` already did it, and the hash round-trip was unnecessary).
- Extracted `assertRefsAbsentFromRemote` and pointed the pre-existing `PolicyBlocked` test at it too, removing a third copy of that block.
- Dropped the `batchCallCount` assertion — already pinned by a sibling test.

## Skipped, with reasons

- **Gate moved inside `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` with a failure-policy enum** (altitude's main recommendation). Structurally better, but I checked `CleanupPushedShadowBranches` and it deletes on session-state protection alone, independent of whether the push landed — so running it on the withhold path, as that restructure would, is a behaviour change I won't make under a cleanup remit.
- **Empty-queue prompt.** Genuinely the sharpest finding: the gate resolves the OPF decision before anything knows the queue is non-empty, so `doctor migrate` can ask "Run OPF? Adds ~30s", get a yes, then print "No queued refs to push". Rare (the command just migrated the refs), pre-existing on the pre-push side, and fixing it changes when a prompt appears — so it's a note for the PR, not a silent change.
- **Queue + ref lookups running twice per flush** — pre-existing; the fix threads state through a shared function well outside this diff. Worth putting in the PR: on reftable repos each `repo.Reference` spawns git subprocesses, so a 200-ref migration backfill pays ~800 avoidable spawns.
- **Egress assertion in `push_common.go`** covering both backends — needs per-process decision plumbing; the reviewer itself scoped it as a follow-up.
- **Guard test** — the reviewer argued against one, and I agree: the required-parameter version would be strictly stronger, and a grep-guard weaker than what the type system already gives here.

Still uncommitted, same two files.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Apply the OPF gate to the queued-checkpoint-ref push

PushQueuedCheckpointRefs flushed the checkpoint-ref push queue with no
OPF gate, so with redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled set, answering
yes to `entire doctor migrate`'s "Push N migrated checkpoint ref(s) now?"
sent 8-layer content to the remote, untagged, without the OPF decision
ever being resolved. That is the OPFSkip outcome without the user having
chosen it.

Give it the same gate the pre-push path has. The shared piece,
runOPFForCheckpointRefs, becomes opfGateForCheckpointRefs and returns an
error instead of a bool so each caller reports failure its own way: the
pre-push hook warns and continues, because a checkpoint failure must

## What was wrong

`PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` (`manual_commit_push.go`) flushed the checkpoint-ref push queue with no OPF gate. Its only production caller is the migration command's opt-in push (`doctor_migrate.go`), so with `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled` set, answering yes to "Push N migrated checkpoint ref(s) now?" sent 8-layer content to the remote, untagged.

A user who enabled OPF and never chose to skip got the skip anyway, and the two answers to the one prompt they did see had opposite safety: "No" left the refs queued for the next `git push`, which applies OPF; "Yes" sent them now, without it.

Scope is the git-refs backend. The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch has its own pre-push OPF rewrite and is unaffected. Pre-existing, not introduced by any open PR.

`PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` gets the same gate `prePushCheckpointRefs` already had, in the same position — after the checkpoint-policy check, before the flush.

This push was explicitly requested, so it errors with the refs left queued — matching how the same function already handles a blocking checkpoint policy, and leaving the next `git push` to apply OPF and deliver them. `redact.OPFEnabled()` moved inside the gate, so a caller cannot half-apply it by remembering the function and forgetting the flag.

`doctor migrate` only reaches this code with a TTY present, so with OPF enabled and no persisted `prompt_default`, answering yes to "Push now?" now shows the standard "Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints?" prompt. Two tests in `refs_push_test.go`, both on the existing `setupGitRefsOPFRepo` fixture so they assert observable state rather than that a function was called. The first pins that the commit reaching the remote is the rewritten one — sentinel scrubbed, `Entire-OPF-Applied` trailer present, remote ref hash equal to the rewritten local hash. The second pins fail-closed: an OPF runtime failure errors, leaves every ref unmoved and queued, and puts nothing on the remote.

Both were written first and confirmed failing against unmodified `main`: two refs reached the bare remote with zero OPF invocations and no trailer, and a deliberately failing OPF runtime did not stop the push either. Re-verified after the cleanup pass by removing the gate again.

The gate sits at both call sites of `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` rather than inside it. Inside — with a required failure-policy argument, so a third caller could not compile without stating its policy — would be structurally better, but it changes when `cleanupPushedShadowBranches` runs on the withhold path, which deletes on session-state protection alone and so needs its own consideration.

The gate resolves the OPF decision before anything knows the queue is non-empty, so an already-drained queue can prompt for a ~30s scan and then report nothing to push. Rare here (the command just migrated the refs) and pre-existing on the pre-push side.

`RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF` and `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` each resolve the queue and partition the refs, so a flush of N refs does two queue reads and 3N `repo.Reference` lookups. 	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/settings"
	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy"
)

func newDoctorMigrateCheckpointsCmd() *cobra.Command {
	var dryRun bool
	var remote string

	cmd := &cobra.Command{
		Use:   "migrate-checkpoints",
		Short: "Convert git-branch checkpoints into per-checkpoint git refs (git-refs store)",
		Long: `Convert the checkpoints stored on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch into
per-checkpoint refs under refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>, the layout the
git-refs checkpoint store uses.

Each checkpoint's current tree is wrapped in a fresh commit and its ref is
pointed at it — existing branch commits are not remapped. The checkpoint's
metadata is normalized for the new layout: the legacy checkpoint_version field
is dropped and session file paths are rewritten relative to the ref. The
command is idempotent: checkpoints already converted are skipped, so it is safe
to re-run after more branch activity.

New refs are queued for push. Run interactively, it asks whether to push them
now; non-interactively it never pushes — the refs stay queued and flush on the
next push once the git-refs store is the configured primary.`,
		Args: cobra.NoArgs,
		RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, _ []string) error {
			ctx := cmd.Context()
			out := cmd.OutOrStdout()

			// Once git-refs is the primary store the refs are authoritative and
			// the v1 branch may lag behind them; re-importing its snapshots
			// could only regress refs, so refuse.
			if cpCfg, _ := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg) { //nolint:errcheck // fail-soft: a bad checkpoints block already surfaces via Open; default to allowing migration
				fmt.Fprintln(out, "The git-refs store is already the primary checkpoint store — nothing to migrate.")
				return nil
			}

			repo, err := strategy.OpenRepository(ctx)

content.text:
Two bot reviews, both legitimate. I verified each against the code rather than taking them at face value, and both are now fixed and pushed.

## Bugbot (high severity) — correct, and it invalidated my fix

> `opfGateForCheckpointRefs` returns immediately when `redact.OPFEnabled()` is false, but `doctor migrate-checkpoints` never runs `EnsureRedactionConfigured`.

This was right, and it's the finding that mattered: **the gate was a no-op on its only production caller.** `EnsureRedactionConfigured` lives in doctor's own `PreRunE`, and Cobra does not inherit `PreRunE` to subcommands — only `PersistentPreRunE`. `newDoctorMigrateCheckpointsCmd` defined none, so the process-global OPF config stayed nil, `OPFEnabled()` read false, and refs still shipped unfiltered after the user answered yes.

My original tests missed it precisely because they call `configureFakeOPF` directly — they proved the gate works *when OPF is configured*, never that it is.

Proved it before fixing: a test that runs the real command with OPF enabled in settings and asserts `OPFEnabled()` afterwards fails on the previous commit. Fixed by giving the subcommand its own `PreRunE`.

One thing I deliberately did **not** do: call `EnsureRedactionConfigured` inside the gate to make it self-sufficient. That looked like the more structural fix, but `setupHookContext` deliberately logs-and-continues on its error (the built-in engine cannot fail to construct, and status/doctor/import/attach are the loud paths). Raising it from the gate would withhold pushes on a condition that's documented as survivable. I named the precondition in the gate's doc instead.

## Copilot — correct, narrower

> Ctrl-C at the OPF prompt returns an error that doesn't satisfy `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)`.

Also right, though I fixed the underlying inconsistency rather than its suggestion. `confirmDoctorFix` maps both `huh.ErrUserAborted` and `context.Canceled` to `(false, nil)` — a clean "Refs stay queued", exit 0. So Ctrl-C at the first prompt was silent while Ctrl-C at the second was an error, for the same gesture with the same outcome. I exported `ErrOPFAbortedByUser` and had the command report it as a decline, rather than wrapping `context.Canceled` — the context isn't actually cancelled, and claiming it is would be a lie the v1 pre-push path would inherit.

## State

Second commit pushed (`30dbebd7b`). `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean, full `test:ci` green. I have **not** replied to either bot on the PR — say the word if you want me to.

Worth noting for your own read of the PR body: it currently claims the fix works on the migrate path, which was only true after this second commit. The description doesn't need editing, but the first commit alone doesn't deliver what it says.

content.content:
Fixes #2204

Persistent checkpoint writers use a per-reference cross-process lock followed by native Git compare-and-swap. The two OPF rewrite paths still used go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`, which does not participate in native Git's reference locking protocol.

A native checkpoint update and an OPF rewrite could therefore both observe the same old value and both report success. When the native transaction committed, it overwrote the OPF result, silently losing an update.

## The fix

Add `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef`, which acquires the existing persistent-ref lock and performs the final compare-and-swap through native `git update-ref`. Route both OPF writers through it:

- the shared `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` rewrite
- per-checkpoint reference rewrites

The potentially expensive OPF scan remains outside the lock. If another writer advances the reference during that scan, the final native CAS rejects the stale rewrite instead of overwriting the newer value.

## Why this approach

Native Git CAS is the correctness boundary: it respects Git's reference locks and guarantees that only one writer can replace the expected old value.

We also acquire Entire's existing per-reference lock. This lets cooperating Entire processes wait for each other instead of producing avoidable conflicts, while native Git still protects against external Git processes.

Using native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>` without Entire's lock was another valid option. It would prevent lost updates, but concurrent Entire writers would fail immediately instead of coordinating through the protocol already used by persistent checkpoint writes.

Larger alternatives, such as centralizing all reference writes or changing go-git's locking behavior, could also solve the problem but would substantially expand the scope and risk of this fix. Using only Entire's lock with go-git would not be sufficient because external Git processes do not honor Entire's lock.

The deliberate behavior change is that an OPF rewrite may now briefly wait or fail safely with a conflict. It can no longer report success and then be silently overwritten.

## Verification

The regression tests start a real native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction, pause it after `prepare` while Git owns the reference lock, and then exercise each OPF rewrite path.

Before the fix, both tests demonstrated the lost-update window:

```text
Error: An error is expected but got nil.
Messages: the OPF rewrite must not report success while a native update owns the ref lock
```

After the fix, the focused regression tests passed ten times under the race detector:

```text
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint 2.034s
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy 7.075s
```

`mise run check` also passed, including formatting, lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and the Vogon and Roger-Roger canary suites.

## Scope

This closes the two OPF call sites identified in #2204. Existing strategy reference writes used for initialization, recovery, and migration are unchanged.

for its own retry message.

a lock and native git update-ref, which adds lock contention as a way to
get here.

content.text:
Yes — real overlap, though not conflicting. The handoff's "unrelated to it" was wrong.

## Where they touch

#2211 (`fix(checkpoint): serialize OPF ref updates`, fixes #2204) changes the final compare-and-swap **inside `RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF`** — the exact function my gate invokes — from go-git's `CheckAndSetReference` to `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef` (Entire's per-ref flock plus native `git update-ref`). So both PRs are OPF-rewrite correctness on the git-refs backend, one line apart.

**No file overlap:** its 12 files and my 5 don't intersect. No identifier collisions either.

## They compose — verified, not assumed

I fetched `pull/2211/head`, merged it into a throwaway branch off mine, and ran the affected packages:

- Merge clean, no conflicts; `go build ./...` OK
- `strategy`, `checkpoint`, and `cli` packages all green, including my two new tests and its two new lost-update regression tests

Temp branch deleted, my branch restored, tree clean. Whoever merges second just rebases.

## What the overlap did expose

#2211 adds a new way for that function to fail: lock contention or a CAS conflict *after* a successful OPF scan. My error message said "OPF did not run, so checkpoint refs stay queued" — wrong in exactly that case, where OPF ran fine and the ref update lost a race. The outcome was still right (nothing shipped, refs stay queued), but the attribution would have sent someone after the wrong problem.

#2211 touches `flock_unix.go`, and your notes record a macOS-only `os.Root` concurrent-openat ENOENT bug (golang/go#81246) that silently broke session-state flock in #2180. Linux CI being green won't clear that. Not my call on that PR, but it's the risk I'd probe before merging it.

content.text:
All three findings hold. I verified each against the PR head (`74cff6839`) and reproduced #1 rather than reasoning about it.

## 1. SIGKILL in the prepared window wedges the ref — confirmed, and worse than stated

`prepareRefCAS` uses `exec.CommandContext` with no `Cancel` and no `WaitDelay`, so Go's default cancel is `Process.Kill()` — SIGKILL. `CompareAndSwapRef` then holds the transaction **prepared** — git owns `.git/refs/<name>.lock` — across a full `git symbolic-ref` fork before committing.

Reproduced on git 2.50.1 (you saw 2.55.0, so it isn't version-specific):

| cancel method | `.lock` left behind | later plain `git update-ref` | transaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SIGKILL** (current default) | **yes** | **fails: "cannot lock ref … File exists"** | aborted |
| SIGTERM | no | succeeds | aborted |
| close stdin | no | succeeds | aborted |

Git's own message confirms there's no recovery: *"remove the file manually to continue."*

Two things worth adding for the author:

- **SIGTERM is sufficient.** Git's tempfile/lockfile signal cleanup removes the lock, so `procutil.TerminateOnCancel` — already in the repo, already SIGTERM-then-SIGKILL-after-`WaitDelay` — fixes this with one line. Closing stdin also works but exits **0**, so the Go side would have to be careful not to read that as success.
- **No variant silently commits.** I checked the ref value after each: all three abort. So the choice is purely about lock hygiene, not about a spurious write.

The window is short (one fork), but the OPF path takes the lock once *per ref*, so a migration backfill has N windows. And `main.go:44-66` confirms SIGINT/SIGTERM call `cancel()` on the root ctx that the pre-push hook runs under — Ctrl-C during `git push` reaches the hook via the foreground process group. Reachable.

## 2. The 2s bound aborts the push instead of delaying it — confirmed

Traced end to end: `withPersistentRefFlockWait` → `DeadlineExceeded` → `atomicSetV1Ref` (it isn't `ErrRefCASConflict`, so it falls through to `fmt.Errorf("set v1 ref: %w")`) → `RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF` → `manual_commit_push.go:164` `return rewriteErr` → non-zero pre-push exit → **push aborted**.

Nothing classifies it and nothing retries it: `retryPersistentRefLockContention` sits *inside* the flock, so it cannot retry a failed acquire. And the constant's own comment names "another writer's potentially expensive checkpoint build" as the expected holder — so it fires exactly in the case it was written for. Trading "the push waits" for "the push dies" is the wrong direction.

Two details to hand over: this hits the **git-branch/v1 backend only** — the refs backend's fail-closed path withholds and returns nil, so it degrades correctly. And the 2s bounds only the *acquire*; the CAS retries afterwards are unbounded, so it doesn't actually cap the hook's contribution to push latency.

## 3. The flock semantic change — confirmed, and the deleted comment promised the opposite

The gate went from `_, hasDeadline := ctx.Deadline(); !hasDeadline` to `ctx.Done() == nil`. The deleted comment said in as many words that a deadline-free context "takes the same blocking kernel path as Acquire, **so existing callers keep their exact behavior**", naming turn-end condensation as a must-wait caller.

Every CLI context is cancelable (root ctx, `main.go:44`), so in practice *only* `context.Background()` now takes the kernel path. Turn-end condensation — the caller that comment singled out — now does 25ms `LOCK_NB` polling.

Beyond the wasted syscalls, the part I'd raise loudest is **fairness**: `LOCK_EX` gives you a kernel queue position; poll-and-retry gives you none. Under the N-agents-one-repo workflow Entire encourages, a poller can be starved by other acquirers indefinitely. This is a shared primitive and the change is invisible in the commit messages.

## One minor addition

`gitPlumbingEnv()` does `append(os.Environ(), …)`, so it inherits `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`, which take precedence over `cmd.Dir`. CLAUDE.md requires `gitrepo.EnvWithoutRepoOverrides()` for any git subprocess that can run inside a hook and names its target via `cmd.Dir` — and `CompareAndSwapRef` does both. All three anchored correctly on the intended lines.

## On merge order — I'd push back slightly

Technically the order doesn't matter: I merged #2211 into my branch locally and it was clean, built, and `strategy` + `checkpoint` + `cli` all passed. Its change to the function my gate calls is one line in a file I don't touch. Whichever lands second rebases in seconds.

So the question is only about sequencing effort, and there the asymmetry runs the other way:

- **#2236 is green and unblocked now.**
- **#2211 has two blockers** that need author turnaround — and one of them (#1) means a Ctrl-C during a pre-push can leave a repo needing manual `.lock` removal, which is a worse day than the lost update it fixes.

Gating my PR on that means an ungated OPF push — refs shipping 8-layer content untagged with no decision resolved — stays on `main` for however long that turnaround takes, in exchange for nothing technical.

My suggestion: **land #2236 now, let #2211 land when its blockers are fixed.** If you'd rather give the external contributor the clean base and land theirs first, that's a fair call too and I'll rebase — I just wouldn't hold the privacy fix behind a PR with open blockers.

One thing that argues mildly for #2211 first if you do wait: my third commit's message references #2211 making the mis-attributed error more likely, which reads more naturally in that order. Cosmetic, not a reason on its own.

Want me to add a note on #2236 pointing at the #2211 relationship either way?

func TestPushMigratedRefs_ConfiguresRedactionBeforeGating(t *testing.T) {
	repo, bareDir := setupMigratePushRepo(t,

All three were correct. Verified each rather than taking them on trust, and all three are fixed in `47566e1f5`.

## 1. Commit 3 was half-done — confirmed

`warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` still said "OPF did not run" for the identical set of causes, on the pre-push channel where nearly every withheld flush is actually reported. Now cause-neutral, matching the error.

One thing that fell out: `test:ci` caught that my first rewording broke an existing assertion (`assert.Contains(buf, "checkpoint refs")` — I'd capitalised it). My earlier grep for the old wording was too narrow to catch it. Rather than weaken that assertion I reworded to keep "checkpoint refs" lowercase, so it still checks what it was written to check.

## 2. `--dry-run` regression — reproduced

Measured both sides with both scanners disabled: `origin/main` returns `nil` and prints "nothing to migrate"; my PR returned `merged settings invalid: invalid redaction scanner configuration…`. Exactly as you described.

The precondition moved from the `PreRunE` into `pushMigratedRefs`, the one path that needs it. `--dry-run`, already-primary, and nothing-migrated all return before it now.

## 3. The test pinned shape, not behaviour — agreed

It executed the subcommand detached from its parent, so it asserted "this command has a `PreRunE`" rather than "redaction is configured when the push gates" — and would have failed on a `PersistentPreRunE` move that changes nothing behaviourally.

Replaced with `TestPushMigratedRefs_ConfiguresRedactionBeforeGating`, which drives the push path directly and touches no cobra wiring, plus a regression test for the `--dry-run` path. I confirmed both go red for the right reason: removing the call from the push path fails the first, restoring the `PreRunE` fails the second.

**One place I went a different way than you suggested.** I didn't move it to doctor's `PersistentPreRunE`. It would cover future subcommands, but it widens finding 2 rather than fixing it — `doctor logs` and `doctor bundle` would newly fail on bad scanner config, and those are what you reach for when the repo is already broken. Scoping the precondition to the push instead makes the guarantee independent of any parent wiring, which is the stronger version of what your finding was after. The trap for a *future* subcommand that pushes checkpoint content does remain; the gate documents the precondition, but nothing enforces it. Say the word if you'd rather have the persistent wiring anyway.

`fmt`/`lint` clean, full `test:ci` green (56 canary + 4 e2e). Four commits on the branch.

Description:
Problem:
The PushQueuedCheckpointRefs function, used by the checkpoint migration command's opt-in "push now" feature, was missing the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OPF) gate that pre-push already enforces. When OPF is enabled, queued checkpoint refs could be pushed without applying the 9-layer OPF redaction, allowing under-redacted content to reach the remote while the main pre-push hook properly gates the regular branch push.
Solution:
Added opfGateForCheckpointRefs as the unified gate for all checkpoint-ref flush paths. The function returns an error (rather than a boolean) when OPF cannot run, making it clear that both pre-push and explicit-push callers must check it before letting refs leave the machine. The gate is now called in PushQueuedCheckpointRefs before flushing the queue, ensuring OPF re-redaction happens regardless of how the push is triggered. Two new tests pin the fix: one verifies that OPF-applied commits with the trailer reach the remote, and another confirms that OPF failures leave refs queued and the remote untouched.

content.text:
## PR #2236 — one thing blocking

Branch `soph/opf-gate-queued-checkpoint-refs`, 5 commits, tree clean and pushed.

| | |
|---|---|
| CI (12 checks) | ✅ all green |
| Approvals gate | ✅ 1/1 (gtrrz-victor) |
| Checks gate | ✅ passed |
| **Findings gate** | ❌ **1 high-severity finding — blocking** |
| Review threads | ✅ all 3 resolved (Bugbot, Copilot, gtrrz-victor) |

That findings gate is why "Entire Gates" shows FAILURE. It's also the answer to my earlier "the trail is clean" — the finding landed at 12:08 yesterday, after I'd checked.

## The finding, and my read of it

On `doctor_migrate_test.go:172-196`, high severity, confidence 0.85.

**It's right about the bug, and it's mine:** `setupMigratePushRepo`'s doc comment says it builds "one queued checkpoint ref" and the implementation never queues one. A false comment I wrote.

**Its conclusion is wrong, though.** It says the test "passes trivially" and "doesn't actually verify the OPF gate". The test's single assertion is that `pushMigratedRefs` calls `EnsureRedactionConfigured` — which doesn't depend on the queue having anything in it, and I confirmed it goes red when that call is removed. Gate-with-real-refs-and-a-real-scan coverage already exists separately in `TestPushQueuedCheckpointRefs_OPFAppliedBeforePush`.

**On its suggested fix I have an honest gap.** I probed queuing a ref as it recommends: it passes and pushes 1 ref. But I could not explain *why* — `opf` is absent from this machine, and the batch scan should have failed closed. I'd rather not build a test on a path whose behaviour I can't account for, especially when it could differ in CI.

So my recommendation is: fix the doc comment to describe what the helper actually builds, and don't queue a ref. That fixes the real defect and leaves the finding's proposed change unmade, with reasons.

## PR #2211

Head moved `74cff6839` → `fc410717c` since my review, so the author has pushed something — I haven't checked whether it addresses the two blocking findings (SIGKILL wedging the ref lock, and the 2s bound aborting the push).

## What I need from you

1. Push the doc-comment fix? It's one line and unambiguously my error.
2. Then resolve the finding with that reasoning, or leave it for gtrrz-victor to judge since it's gating the merge and I'm partly disagreeing with it?
3. Want me to re-review #2211 at its new head?

input.statusReason:
Right that the doc comment was false — it claimed "one queued checkpoint ref" and the helper queues none. Fixed in 7c0bc1dea by correcting the comment rather than making it true.

Not adopting the suggested change, with a reason. The test's only assertion is that pushMigratedRefs calls EnsureRedactionConfigured, which runs ahead of the flush and so does not depend on the queue; removing that call makes it fail, which is verified. So it is not passing trivially — it just is not the test for the gate's behaviour.

Queuing a ref would also be fragile rather than stronger. I probed it: it passes and pushes 1 ref, even though `opf` is absent here. The reason is that redact.BatchBytesWithPrivacyFilter only shells out for leaves containing a space (batch.go:76, gated on len(batchInputs) > 0), and this fixture's content ("init", plus JSON with no spaced values) yields none. So the OPF scan never runs — queuing a ref adds a real flush but still no real scan, and the test would start requiring a real OPF binary the moment someone puts a space in the fixture.

Gate coverage with real queued refs and a real scan already exists in TestPushQueuedCheckpointRefs_OPFAppliedBeforePush, which uses the sentinel-bearing setupGitRefsOPFRepo fixture with a fake OPF runtime and asserts the trailer, the scrubbed sentinel, and that the rewritten commit is the one on the remote.

Persistent checkpoint writers use a per-reference cross-process lock followed by native Git compare-and-swap. The two OPF rewrite paths still used go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`, which does not participate in native Git's reference locking protocol.

A native checkpoint update and an OPF rewrite could therefore both observe the same old value and both report success. When the native transaction committed, it overwrote the OPF result, silently losing an update.

## The fix

Add `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef`, which acquires the existing persistent-ref lock and performs the final compare-and-swap through native `git update-ref`. Route both OPF writers through it:

- the shared `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` rewrite
- per-checkpoint reference rewrites

The potentially expensive OPF scan remains outside the lock. If another writer advances the reference during that scan, the final native CAS rejects the stale rewrite instead of overwriting the newer value.

## Why this approach

Native Git CAS is the correctness boundary: it respects Git's reference locks and guarantees that only one writer can replace the expected old value.

We also acquire Entire's existing per-reference lock. This lets cooperating Entire processes wait for each other instead of producing avoidable conflicts, while native Git still protects against external Git processes.

Using native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>` without Entire's lock was another valid option. It would prevent lost updates, but concurrent Entire writers would fail immediately instead of coordinating through the protocol already used by persistent checkpoint writes.

Larger alternatives, such as centralizing all reference writes or changing go-git's locking behavior, could also solve the problem but would substantially expand the scope and risk of this fix. Using only Entire's lock with go-git would not be sufficient because external Git processes do not honor Entire's lock.

The deliberate behavior change is that an OPF rewrite may now briefly wait or fail safely with a conflict. It can no longer report success and then be silently overwritten.

## Verification

The regression tests start a real native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction, pause it after `prepare` while Git owns the reference lock, and then exercise each OPF rewrite path.

Before the fix, both tests demonstrated the lost-update window:

```text
Error: An error is expected but got nil.
Messages: the OPF rewrite must not report success while a native update owns the ref lock
```

After the fix, the focused regression tests passed ten times under the race detector:

```text
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint 2.034s
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy 7.075s
```

`mise run check` also passed, including formatting, lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and the Vogon and Roger-Roger canary suites.

## Scope

This closes the two OPF call sites identified in #2204. Existing strategy reference writes used for initialization, recovery, and migration are unchanged.

Persistent checkpoint writers use a per-reference cross-process lock followed by native Git compare-and-swap. The two OPF rewrite paths still used go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`, which does not participate in native Git's reference locking protocol.

A native checkpoint update and an OPF rewrite could therefore both observe the same old value and both report success. When the native transaction committed, it overwrote the OPF result, silently losing an update.

## The fix

Add `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef`, which acquires the existing persistent-ref lock and performs the final compare-and-swap through native `git update-ref`. Route both OPF writers through it:

- the shared `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` rewrite
- per-checkpoint reference rewrites

The potentially expensive OPF scan remains outside the lock. If another writer advances the reference during that scan, the final native CAS rejects the stale rewrite instead of overwriting the newer value.

## Why this approach

Native Git CAS is the correctness boundary: it respects Git's reference locks and guarantees that only one writer can replace the expected old value.

We also acquire Entire's existing per-reference lock. This lets cooperating Entire processes wait for each other instead of producing avoidable conflicts, while native Git still protects against external Git processes.

Using native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>` without Entire's lock was another valid option. It would prevent lost updates, but concurrent Entire writers would fail immediately instead of coordinating through the protocol already used by persistent checkpoint writes.

Larger alternatives, such as centralizing all reference writes or changing go-git's locking behavior, could also solve the problem but would substantially expand the scope and risk of this fix. Using only Entire's lock with go-git would not be sufficient because external Git processes do not honor Entire's lock.

The deliberate behavior change is that an OPF rewrite may now briefly wait or fail safely with a conflict. It can no longer report success and then be silently overwritten.

## Verification

The regression tests start a real native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction, pause it after `prepare` while Git owns the reference lock, and then exercise each OPF rewrite path.

Before the fix, both tests demonstrated the lost-update window:

```text
Error: An error is expected but got nil.
Messages: the OPF rewrite must not report success while a native update owns the ref lock
```

After the fix, the focused regression tests passed ten times under the race detector:

```text
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint 2.034s
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy 7.075s
```

`mise run check` also passed, including formatting, lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and the Vogon and Roger-Roger canary suites.

## Scope

This closes the two OPF call sites identified in #2204. Existing strategy reference writes used for initialization, recovery, and migration are unchanged.

Both done.

## The trail finding — looked at, and it's the same single one

Re-polled with every filter relaxed: still exactly one, `01M1H0A7JGCA7MMBTGS0YFC3VY`. It's the one from my status message, not a new one.

**I closed the gap I'd flagged**, which changed the answer. I couldn't previously explain why queuing a ref passed with no `opf` binary installed. The mechanism is `redact/batch.go:76`: the OPF shell-out is gated on `len(batchInputs) > 0`, and only leaves *containing a space* become batch inputs. This fixture's content (`"init"`, plus JSON with no spaced values) yields none, so OPF is never invoked.

That turns my hedge into a concrete argument: adopting the finding's suggestion would add a real flush but still no real scan, **and** would make the test require a real OPF binary the moment anyone puts a space in the fixture.

So I split it:
- **Fixed** the actual defect — the doc comment claimed "one queued checkpoint ref" and queued none (`7c0bc1dea`). Corrected the comment rather than making it true, with the reasoning recorded there.
- **Declined** the suggested change, and **resolved** the finding with that mechanism written into the status reason so it's auditable. That unblocks the findings gate. If you'd rather gtrrz-victor arbitrate, it can be reopened — I resolved it because the actionable part was genuinely fixed and the rest is now evidence-backed rather than a judgement call.

## #2211 review kicked off
